Counting the cells, I get shapes of sizes 3, 4, 5, 5, and 8, totaling 25 cells, which matches a single group of five shapes filling a 5x5 grid. Now I need to figure out how these pieces can tile that grid with rotations allowed.

I'm placing the 8-cell piece across the top three rows first, leaving a 17-cell remainder to fill with the tromino and two pentominoes, then working through which orientations of the V-pentomino and Y-pentomino could fit the leftover notch-shaped region.

That checks out: 3+4+5=12. Now (4,4) needs coverage since (3,4) is taken, so I need a shape extending along row4 into it, leaving the tromino, tetromino, and one pentomino to fill remaining space. I'm testing the 2-pentomino with a bump shape rotated to fit along row4 starting around column 1.

Both bump orientations for that piece keep landing on cells already occupied by V, so I'm hunting for another placement that avoids the conflict.

Maybe I should back up and place piece 3 somewhere else entirely, then re-derive which cells remain uncovered in each row before trying piece 8 again.

That column-4 idea doesn't work since (1,3) is taken by the 8-shape already. Let me try piece 7 instead: cells (1,4),(2,4),(3,4),(3,3) as a vertical-with-foot tetromino matches the col4 rows1-3 plus (3,3) shape exactly, so I'll use that placement and check what's left in row1.

Now I need to place pieces 2, 3, and 5 into the remaining cells. Corner cell (4,4) can only connect through (4,3), so I try piece 2 as a base along row4 cols1-4 with a bump at (3,2), which fits since that cell is open, leaving a smaller remaining region for pieces 3 and 5. For piece 3 (V-shaped), I'm checking whether the leftover column-0 cells rows1-4 plus adjacent cells can form the needed 3+3 arm shape.

I try a V using (1,0),(1,1),(1,2) horizontally with (2,0),(3,0) vertically, but the leftover cells (2,1),(3,1),(4,0) don't connect into a valid tromino, so that fails.

Trying a different fifth piece: an L-tromino at (4,0),(3,0),(3,1) leaves (1,0),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1) forming a P-pentomino instead of a V, so that fails too.

I revisit how piece 2 covers (4,4): the row-4 bump variant is already tried, so I check V and L configurations through (4,2)-(4,4) and (3,4), but most neighboring cells are already taken, forcing me toward another 5-tromino attempt near (4,4),(4,3),(3,...).

That last attempt collides with the piece labeled 7, so I need to backtrack and try a different placement for either piece 7 or piece 8. For piece 7 I check the column-4 option using (1,4),(2,4),(3,4), and (1,3) is fine since it's unoccupied there. Then for piece 8, I try rotating it 180 degrees, which reshapes it into a row-1 block of two cells, a single cell in row1, and a full row2 — I start placing this rotated version starting from row 2.

Placing the rotated 8 leaves an irregular set of open cells across rows 0-3, and I count them up to confirm they total 17, matching what's needed for the remaining pieces (V-pentomino, tetromino, and tromino). Working through it, I find the V-pentomino fits nicely along column 4 rows 1-3 plus two cells in row 3, leaving row 0 completely open for the next piece to cover.

Trying to place a pentomino across row 0 keeps stranding an isolated cell near (2,3) or (0,4), so I test shifting the bump position, but each variant leaves some cell without a valid neighbor. I conclude that (2,3) must pair with (1,3), so I try building the tetromino as a vertical strip down column 3 combined with an adjacent cell to keep everything connected.

Let me actually compute the rotation coordinates for this piece to verify which orientation it produces.

Rotating the shape 180 degrees gives a vertical column with an extra cell at the top-right, and rotating 270 degrees gives a horizontal bar with an extra cell at the bottom-right. I need to check which of these rotations matches the vertical pair I already have at the target location.

That leaves a bare straight tromino for piece 5, but piece 5 is an L-shape, so this placement fails. Trying (3,0),(2,0),(1,0) as part of a bigger piece also runs into occupied neighbors, so I need to back up and try different V/7 placements in this configuration.

Reconsidering config A with 8 occupying rows 0-2, cols 0-4, I look at the forced vertical chain through (1,4),(2,4),(3,4) since (1,4)'s only open neighbor is (2,4). I'm testing a 7-piece running vertically down column 4 rows 1-3 with an extra cell at bottom-left (3,3).

I'm placing the shape with a bump at (3,3), then fitting the V-shape into the remaining space using cells at rows 2-4, and checking what's left to cover the final cells.

Trying tromino placements around (4,3), I find one that works: an L-shape at (4,2),(4,3),(3,2), leaving the 7-piece to fit vertically along column 1 rows 2-4 plus (4,0), matching its original orientation. That gives a valid full tiling — config A — so I start laying out the remaining rows.

I finalize all the placements and verify by checking every cell in the 5x5 grid row by row against the shape assignments, and everything checks out consistently. Now I'm wondering whether the orientation of each shape needs to match its original given orientation exactly, since that constraint affects how the output should be reported.

Input 7 matches its tiling orientation exactly, but inputs 2 and 3 need rotation checks against their tilings—I'm comparing normalized coordinates for each shape piece by piece.

Now I'm laying out the base 5x5 square with its color pattern, then plan to test each of the four rotations against each anchor to find which orientation matches the input arrangement.

Finishing the CW90 rotation row by row, then starting on the CW180 rotation by reversing rows and columns.

Continuing the CW270 rotation, I finish computing the remaining rows, then start checking anchors: the 8-shape in B keeps the same orientation as the input, appearing at rows19-21, cols5-9 with origin (19,5).

Working out where the 8's cells sit in B versus input, I place the square at rows19-23, cols5-9, which fits within the grid's height. I then check the 7-shape, finding it matches orientation too and calculating the offset places its square at rows1-5, cols18-22, which also fits. I'm now starting to map the 5-shape's cell positions in the input.

With min row 4, min col 8, the square spans rows 4-8, cols 7-11.

Now checking anchor 2: normalizing input cells gives (0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(0,3),(1,2), and comparing against B's shape and its 90-degree rotation to find a matching orientation.

Testing the 90-degree rotation, I get cells with a bump above at index1, but the input has its bump below at index2, so that's not a match. Trying 180-degree rotation, I get a vertical arrangement with a right bump at row1, which is also not horizontal like the input, so that fails too. Now testing 270-degree rotation...

Let me verify: this normalized set matches the input pattern exactly, so I should use the 270-degree grid, calculating the offset between the pattern's minimum coordinates and the input's minimum coordinates to place the square correctly at rows10-14, cols2-6.

Now checking the 3-cells anchor pattern against the input's normalized coordinates - the 90 and 180 rotations don't match, so I'm now testing the CW90 rotation for this shape.

This matches, so I calculate the offset for the CW90 square placement at rows12-16, cols14-18. Now I need to compose the full 26x25 output grid and check each transformed square's placement region for potential overlaps.

I confirm there are no overlaps between the five placed squares, so drawing order doesn't matter for the final result. Now I'm working out the actual grid values for the 180-rotated square and verifying they align with the original input cells at rows4-8, cols7-11.

Checking the rot0 B square placement at rows19-23, cols5-9, I verify the 8s and other values match against the input grid.

Now I'm figuring out where the rot0 B square lands at rows1-5, cols18-22, mapping its first row of all 8s onto that region.

I confirm the 7 values at (3,19), (4,19), and (5,18)/(5,19) line up correctly with the rotated block.

Moving to the 270-degree rotated grid, I'm verifying rows10-14, cols2-6 against the input, checking the 2s at row10 and row11 match.

Now I'm working through a CW90 rotated grid at rows12-16, cols14-18, starting to check the values against expected input positions.

With all block placements verified, I'm now assembling the final output grid row by row, filling in zeros for empty rows and the specific column values (8s, 3s, 2s, 5s, 7s) for the populated rows across the 18-22 and 7-11 column ranges, then continuing into the 2-6 column range for later rows.

Now I'm assembling each row into full 25-column arrays based on this grid data.

I'm looking at the worked example again — the 5-cell and 4-cell pieces forming a 3x3, and the larger pieces forming a 5x5 — to confirm both partitions are genuinely unique packings. I want to reuse that same piece pair at different positions or rotations, but I'm wary that the earlier empty-output examples might just be noise contradicting the correct demonstrations, so I need enough correct cases to make the real pattern dominate.

Right, two objects alone won't satisfy the minimum group size, so I need at least three shapes total — better to use two separate rigid pairs, four objects in all. For demo A I'll keep the 1/7 pair as one group, then add a second pair with distinct signatures: an R/S pair inside a 4x4 grid where S is a 2x2 square anchor and R is its complement, making sure the placement giving a valid rigid match is unique among the possible anchor positions.

I need pieces whose rotation set is genuinely limited — the P/Q pair from the example seems to work, so I'm considering reusing that same pair structure, or the 5x5 staircase pair, across both demos but in different orientations.

I'm also trying to construct a new rigid pair in a 4x4 grid: a 10-cell triangular staircase piece and its 6-cell triangular complement, checking whether the complement placement is forced given the anchor's bounding box constraints.

Confirming this pair is rigid since both pieces' bounding boxes fill the full 4x4, forcing unique placement regardless of which one anchors, and their cell counts differ enough to distinguish them by signature. Now I'm setting up a test grid combining the earlier 3x3 P/Q pair with this new 4x4 triangle pair at varied positions and rotations to verify everything works together.

Checking B's bounding square at rows8-11 cols8-11, and P/Q anchored squares at rows1-3 cols1-3 and cols9-11 respectively — all fit correctly. Ready to test.
